How to build a Python DSL

slides.title: How do we produce MLIR?
slides.notes: Start with the two existing tools: hand-written textual IR and MLIR Python bindings. Text is useful for exact tests but is static; variations require edits or a generator. Bindings let Python generate arbitrary IR, but the author still wires up types, context, insertion points, lowering, the execution engine and argument packing. Do not introduce the DSL solution yet.

items.title: Write MLIR by hand
items.body: Static text. Every variant is manual.

items.title: Use the Python bindings
items.body: Generate IR. Wire up compilation and execution.

slides.title: Just a + b, with Python bindings
slides.caption: Complete program: build IR → lower → JIT → call.
slides.notes: The entire runnable scalar addition program appears here, including every import, context, type, operation, lowering pass, C-interface attribute, ExecutionEngine construction and ctypes invocation. Read the panels from left to right: the second continues inside the same Context. Both inputs are i32; 2 + 3 prints 5. This demonstrates infrastructure cost, not a performance comparison. No PyTorch or DSL code appears on this slide.

left.label: 1 · Build the IR
left.code:
import ctypes as C
from mlir import ir, execution_engine as ee
from mlir import passmanager as pm
from mlir.dialects import arith, func

with ir.Context(), ir.Location.unknown():
    i32 = ir.IntegerType.get_signless(32)
    module = ir.Module.create()
    with ir.InsertionPoint(module.body):
        fn = func.FuncOp(
            "add", ([i32, i32], [i32]))
        fn.attributes["llvm.emit_c_interface"] = (
            ir.UnitAttr.get())
        entry = fn.add_entry_block()
        with ir.InsertionPoint(entry):
            a, b = fn.arguments
            result = arith.AddIOp(a, b).result
            func.ReturnOp([result])

right.label: 2 · Compile + execute
right.code:
pipeline = (
        "builtin.module("
        "convert-arith-to-llvm,"
        "convert-func-to-llvm,"
        "reconcile-unrealized-casts)"
    )
    pm.PassManager.parse(pipeline).run(
        module.operation)
    engine = ee.ExecutionEngine(module)

    a, b = C.c_int32(2), C.c_int32(3)
    out = C.c_int32()
    engine.invoke(
        "add", C.byref(a), C.byref(b),
        C.byref(out))
    print(out.value)  # 5

slides.notes: Left: ordinary PyTorch CPU float32 tensors and the desired elementwise addition. Right: the full mlir dsl program, with imports, Pointer annotation, staged length, native loop and call. Read both panels as one program, left then right. This is the interface we want users to write: the reference mlir dsl selects plugins that generate, lower, cache and invoke the program. Pointers and explicit sizes are the current host boundary, not an Array wrapper. The example runs on the CPU and makes no GPU or tensor-library performance claim.

slides.title: Four use cases inside NVIDIA
slides.notes: Four use cases supplied by Guray from NVIDIA work: generate internal dialect inputs directly for tests; emit recipe-only IR for a consumer that is not an MLIR compiler; reuse JIT cache, naming and environment infrastructure in another DSL; build a complete user-facing language. The public product example is NVIDIA CuTe DSL / CUTLASS Python; the hyperlink is official documentation. The first three are internal motivations without naming a confidential dialect. Keep this as a visual motivation, not a list of unsupported product claims.

slides.title: How do we build mlir dsl?
slides.notes: Ask the design questions before introducing the solution. MLIR is compiler infrastructure, not one fixed end-to-end compiler. Compiler A and B may choose unrelated dialects and lowering pipelines. Control-flow models also differ: a direct scf.for has no break operation, while scf.while can express termination and another dialect may model early exits differently. We need to reuse frontend infrastructure without hard-wiring these target decisions.

items.title: Which dialects?
items.body: Every compiler has its own IR.

items.title: Generate IR—or execute?
items.body: There is no single end-to-end pipeline.

slides.title: Share the core services
slides.notes: The core owns reusable orchestration and language policy. The four boxes are services, not plugin kinds. BaseDSL begins with an empty Plugins record: it supplies no default target dialect or compiler and is not by itself an end-to-end language. The AST integration hooks live in the core; actual syntax capture is supplied by an optional plugin. Concrete IR operations and compilation are selected by the DSL author.
slides.caption: Core services only. No default dialect or compiler.

slides.title: What is a plugin?
slides.notes: Define plugin before listing its kinds. For staged integer wrappers, operator + calls the selected type-operations implementation. An arith-backed plugin emits arith.addi; an author-supplied dialect plugin could instead emit a matching custom operation, shown illustratively as your.add. The DSL author selects a compatible implementation; this is not runtime dispatch or a claim that arbitrary dialects work automatically. Ordinary Python integers still add in Python. Other plugins provide function entries, control-flow capture, compilation, decorators and adapters; introduce the exact record after these features have been taught.
slides.definition: A replaceable implementation of part of your DSL.
slides.caption: Same Python expression. Your DSL chooses the emitted IR.

slides.title: Compose the DSL you need
slides.notes: Compose a reusable core with the plugins needed for a concrete language. IR generation selects type operations and a function entry, with control-flow capture if required. The compiler is optional: an IR-only DSL can feed an external consumer. Execution additionally needs a compiler implementation and a compatible sub-DSL-owned pipeline. mlir dsl is the runnable showcase using the shipped plugins. Your DSL can reuse those implementations; the core does not itself force an end-to-end target. Exact plugin roles will be introduced beside the later Plugins record.
slides.caption: mlir dsl is a working composition. Reuse its plugins.

slides.title: How much Python should we implement?
slides.notes: Compare ownership, not absolute expressive power. A broad AST-based frontend interprets or lowers supported Python constructs and owns those semantics; it can target many dialects. This design chooses tracing to reuse the interpreter for objects, imports, method dispatch and metaprogramming. Plugins supply the target operations. Tracing alone does not intercept native staged if/for/while; optional limited AST capture handles that syntax. The following design principles and multi-stage slides explain the resulting model.
slides.caption: Our choice: tracing. Optional AST capture handles staged control flow.

slides.title: Design principles
slides.notes: Use Python as the unchanged host language for metaprogramming. Reuse objects, imports and libraries. Only explicit DSL values/operations generate MLIR. The frontend mechanism is modular and target-dialect agnostic; one reusable core underpins multiple sub-DSL namespaces.

slides.title: What is multi-stage programming?
slides.notes: Python is the meta-language and MLIR the object language. The repetition row is an illustration of programs generating later-stage programs, not a claim of an infinite compiler loop. Here the Python interpreter runs the generator, producing MLIR. mlir-opt represents transformation passes; LLVM code generation/JIT creates executable code. The traditional and multi-stage source/compiler/binary icons have identical sizes.

slides.title: Why multi-stage programming?
slides.notes: Use all of Python for trace-time work; capture explicitly through the selected DSL namespace and its typed values. Ordinary range over known values executes as Python; m.range forces staged range construction in the reference namespace. This binding-time boundary enables objects/dictionaries to specialize a program without runtime Python on the generated code path.

slides.title: Agenda
slides.notes: Walk the feature inventory in order: tracing JIT; two kinds of values; numeric and aggregate types; native control flow and explicit builders; arguments; kernels; compilation; caches; trace-only; diagnostics; locations/remarks; observability; sub-DSL authoring. Then hand off to Amir for his material and return for the five-slide Tile design sketch.

slides.title: 1 · Tracing JIT
slides.notes: The core owns @jit and orchestration. Selected func.Entry builds func.func; type_ops emits scalar operations; compiler lowers and invokes the chosen pipeline. Subsequent identical specializations reuse the compiled callable. The host scalar result is a Numeric wrapper; int/float/.value unwrap it. This reference end-to-end path is not provided by an empty BaseDSL.

right.label: Reference execution path
right.code:
Python call
    ↓
Trace func.func
    ↓
Compile + cache

Invoke

slides.title: 2 · Python value or MLIR value?
slides.notes: Two kinds of values: Python payloads compute now; MLIR-backed leaves build staged operations. A DSL annotation makes a runtime argument; ordinary Python configuration is Meta. The implementation additionally stages adapted values containing registered leaves even without annotations, so do not describe annotations as the only rule. is_mlir_op is the predicate. A Numeric wrapper may itself hold a Python literal or an SSA value. There is no Constexpr marker.

left.label: Python

right.label: Generated MLIR · excerpt
right.code:
# At trace time
factor == 3

# In the generated program
%x : i32
%c3 = arith.constant 3 : i32
%r = arith.muli %x, %c3 : i32

slides.title: Python is the metaprogram
slides.notes: Dictionary and values are known configuration; accesses and ordinary functions run in Python. Runtime x is MLIR-backed, so multiply/add emit operations. This is a conceptual variant of the checked affine example; no runtime dictionary is needed.

left.label: Python · implementation excerpt

slides.title: Objects + dictionaries → arithmetic
slides.notes: An ordinary dictionary of Meta objects selects AddN and MulN by Python dispatch. The recipe loop runs while tracing. Each apply receives an MLIR-backed scalar, and only its arithmetic is captured. The same source was checked on the current October7 implementation: int(pipeline(4,ops)) is18. No runtime virtual dispatch or dictionary lookup is emitted. Mutable Meta configuration is legal; staged records crossing regions have different restrictions.

left.label: Python polymorphism

right.label: Metaprogram

slides.takeaway: No runtime dictionary or virtual dispatch.

slides.title: 3 · Numeric types are core policy
slides.notes: These are the wrapper families in types/typing.py. Promotion and conversion policy live in Python. Representation support does not guarantee every host ABI or arithmetic operation for every narrow/wide type. TypeOps maps each dtype to the chosen physical MLIR type; outside a trace use scalar_mlir_type or ask a plugin explicitly, not Int32.mlir_type.

slides.title: Literal → promotion → cast
slides.notes: Python literal defaults are bool→Boolean, int→Int32 (Int64 when outside i32 range), float→Float32. Wrappers with Python payloads can fold in Python. On staged use, the selected type_ops plugin materializes operations. Signed i32+i64 promotes; explicit narrowing truncates and is not universally an error. Narrow Python integer construction may wrap and warn. Runtime x.to(int) raises PHASE_REQUIRES_CONSTANT. Examples show TypeOps with arith, not a plugin named LLVM.

slides.title: The same dtype can target another dialect
slides.notes: Short excerpt based on example14. Imports, scalar_type, tensor constant construction and custom pipeline are omitted; all are required in the full example. The checked full example emits i32 under the reference DSL and rank-zero tensor<i32> under the alternate type_ops plugin. It is a stand-in for a target such as cuda_tile, not actual Tile IR execution. The alternate path is trace-only because its custom lowering is not implemented. TypeOps composes scalar/vector/memory op modules; each part is optional.

left.label: Type-ops plugin · implementation excerpt

slides.title: 4 · Vectors, pointers, structs
slides.notes: Vector and Pointer delegate to type_ops. Host pointers wrap buffers; the default memory module emits LLVM pointer operations. Struct is a frozen pytree record rather than an aggregate SSA type and needs no type-ops hook. Native call/region boundaries flatten and reconstruct leaves. The func entry ABI may separately pack results, which does not change the language value model.

slides.title: Records flatten into their fields
slides.notes: Frozen @struct records flatten at calls and control-flow boundaries. norm2 receives two f32 leaves. The displayed IR is a body/interface sketch; actual host result ABI is owned by func.Entry. The checked current structs example returns norm2=25, with Numeric wrappers for scalar leaves. General frozen dataclasses also work; mutable staged records are rejected. Meta objects need not be frozen.

left.label: Dialect-neutral record

right.label: Two fields → two SSA arguments

slides.takeaway: Frozen record · no aggregate SSA type

slides.title: Extend values with mydialect.Tensor
slides.notes: The staged-only Tensor wrapper demonstrates the exact keyword-only register_leaf API: ir_types, ir_values and from_ir_values. Imports are omitted. Without marshal it is a staged-only leaf, not a host tensor adapter. It can cross staged region boundaries through extracted/rebuilt SSA leaves. Host adaptation requires the additional marshal/adapter contract. Registration happens once at module import. A dialect module supplies operations; a custom value class alone is not a plugin.

left.label: Custom leaf · implementation excerpt

slides.title: 5 · Native control flow
slides.notes: Tracing handles expressions, not Python keywords by operator overload alone. The optional ASTPreprocessorPlugin owns the rewrite and executor callbacks. The shipped scf.ASTPreprocessor pairs the generic syntax rewrite with SCF executors and builders. Meta conditions/bounds execute Python; MLIR-backed values build regions. A different role implementation can capture syntax for another control-flow dialect. No separate SCF dialect plugin exists now; lowering is listed in the sub-DSL pipeline.
slides.takeaway: Syntax capture and IR emission are separate choices.

slides.title: Assigned name → iter_arg
slides.notes: Assignment analysis identifies acc as a carried name. The selected executor flattens carries, creates region arguments, yields updates and rebuilds loop results. This is symbolic analysis of source names, not arbitrary mutation tracking. Current native-control-flow and TYPE_UNSTABLE_JOIN diagnostics pass. More general aliasing and mutation are the subject of Amir’s separate section.

left.label: Python · find the carry
left.code:
acc = m.Int32(0)
for i in range(n):
    acc = acc + i

# Defined outside: acc
# Written inside:  acc

slides.title: Capture has an explicit boundary
slides.notes: The current preprocessor leaves an if/while owning return/raise/break/continue as Python, requiring a Meta condition when reached. Data-dependent early exits are not supported by this frontend. This restriction belongs to the selected preprocessor, not to every possible MLIR program. Captured staged records must be frozen; ordinary Meta objects can remain mutable. Comparisons, ternaries, and/or/not/any/all/min/max/range are handled by the selected capture implementation.

slides.title: Replace capture through one role
slides.notes: The checked CountingPreprocessor test uses this executors override shape to wrap staged loop construction. Here my_loop_executor is a downstream function omitted from the excerpt. Replacing callbacks can target another region dialect when its semantics fit; more extensive capture/early-exit changes may require a different preprocessor_class. This is not a promise that changing one callback supports every target control-flow feature.

left.label: AST plugin · implementation excerpt
left.code:
class MyAST(scf.ASTPreprocessor):
    def executors(self, dsl):
        hooks = super().executors(dsl)
        hooks["loop_execute_range_dynamic"] = (
            my_loop_executor)
        return hooks

# In the Plugins record:
ast_preprocessor=MyAST()

slides.title: 6 · Explicit builders
slides.notes: Explicit builders live with the SCF AST plugin implementation and can be used without enabling its source rewrite. Loop carry values are explicit. This is the sum_of_squares shape from example08. The complete source and other builders are linked; no native AST reconstruction is required for this function.

left.label: Python · implementation excerpt

slides.title: 7 · Bring host values to the DSL
slides.notes: core/arguments.py owns binding/adaptation and the common registry. NumPy arrays and supported dataclass/tuple/list structures adapt to leaves. PyTorch and DLPack are optional AdapterPlugin implementations. DLPack preserves producer lifetime and validates supported dtype/device/contiguity. Dimensions are explicit arguments rather than an automatic Array descriptor. JAX can enter through the protocol when supported; no framework-specific JAX execution claim. The opening PyTorch comparison is checked in v14.
slides.footnote: Pointer ABI: contiguous buffers · dimensions passed separately

slides.title: Adapters work in both directions
slides.notes: Inbound adapters register host-value conversions; outbound adapters may attach ABI wrappers to the traced module, finalize after lowering, and wrap the callable. These hooks belong to AdapterPlugin, not bare Plugin. TVM-FFI is optional and enabled through the DSL environment. Plugin availability is resolved per instance; absent optional dependencies are recorded. No new TVM-FFI execution claim is made here.

slides.title: 8 · @kernel comes from a decorator plugin
slides.notes: The core knows @jit. gpu.Kernels is a DecoratorPlugin that adds @kernel and its deferred launcher, per-trace gpu.module management and host-boundary checks. The three-dot role comment is omitted configuration, not a complete Plugins record. This body assumes a launch covering valid device memory; the next slide uses exactly32 threads on a32-element buffer. GPU tracing can be checked without claiming execution.

left.label: GPU plugin + kernel · excerpt

slides.title: Launch is an explicit operation
slides.notes: Calling the decorated kernel prepares a KernelLauncher; launch emits gpu.launch_func. LaunchConfig normalizes grid/block and dynamic grids are guarded against zero extents. The GPU plugin checks target architecture and host/device buffer kinds. The caller owns device allocation. Reference GPU execution requires a configured target, CUDA runtime and device buffer; this deck treats it as a tracing/source example unless separate GPU evidence is recorded.

left.label: Python · implementation excerpt
left.code:
@m.jit
def run(p: m.Pointer[m.Float32]):
    add_one(p).launch(
        m.LaunchConfig(
            grid=[1], block=[32]))

# Caller owns a 32-element CUDA buffer.
run(device_tensor)

slides.title: 9 · The DSL owns the pass pipeline
slides.notes: Every sub-DSL lists its own pass pipeline in order. No plugin publishes pipeline_passes or contributes an implicit pass list. The selected compiler consumes that list, builds its runtime/engine and loads the entry. The shipped compiler uses MLIR pass manager and ExecutionEngine; another target can replace the whole compiler role. Func entry packs/unpacks results independently of the compiler.

slides.title: Compile now. Call later.
slides.notes: The current API is plain m.compile(function,*representative_args), not bracket flags. It compiles a decorated function without running it and returns a callable. Runtime leaves fix the signature; Python values fix specialization and are checked at later calls. This is ahead-of-call compilation, not a generic standalone binary export API.

left.label: Python · implementation excerpt

slides.title: 10 · Cache compilation work
slides.notes: In-memory cache keys incorporate the traced module identity and relevant compilation configuration. On-disk cache stores lowered bytecode with CRC32 validation; loading it is a file-cache hit rather than a miss. The current cache example passed memory counters (1 hit,3 misses) and a second-process file hit. Do not describe the file cache as a permanent native-binary artifact or claim every arbitrary compiler version/target mismatch is magically handled.

slides.title: 11 · Generate IR and stop
slides.notes: An IR-only DSL still chooses the operations/types and entry needed to build its program. This excerpt omits constructor/imports and uses no native staged control flow; preprocessing must be disabled or supplied by an AST plugin. A missing compiler returns the trace result like DRYRUN, while explicit compile is an error. PRINT_IR displays generated IR. This is a first-class fit for two motivating use cases, not a failed JIT.

left.label: IR-only DSL · setup excerpt
left.code:
class RecipeDSL(BaseDSL):
    plugins = Plugins(
        type_ops=TypeOps(scalars=arith),
        func_entry=func.Entry(),
        compiler=None,
    )

# Or use an existing DSL:
# MLIR_DSL_DRYRUN=1 MLIR_DSL_PRINT_IR=1

slides.title: 12 · Errors should point to Python
slides.notes: User program errors use DSLUserCodeError; runtime/configuration failures use DSLRuntimeError. The renderer formats stable DiagId catalog entries, placeholders, source frames and suggestions. The current diagnostics example passed argument mismatch, early exit, unstable join and closure-capture errors; the old v8 diagnostic mismatch is no longer current. int(x) or x.to(int) on a staged scalar requires a Meta value.

left.label: Python · implementation excerpt

slides.title: 13 · Locations and remarks
slides.notes: core/user_op.py creates traceback-derived locations under DEBUGINFO; core/remarks.py connects collection through the selected compiler remark session. Remarks are structured feedback, not exceptions. The current checkout contains MLIR remark APIs, but this tutorial does not claim they are already in an upstream release. Preserve source coordinates through generated operations for useful errors.
rows: Diagnostics point back to the function

slides.title: 14 · See what the compiler does
slides.notes: The name passed to BaseDSL chooses the environment prefix. These environment names were checked in the current core/env_manager.py. LOG_LEVEL requires LOG_TO_CONSOLE or LOG_TO_FILE to enable a sink. Configuration, logging and compiler timing are inherited infrastructure, while a downstream DSL can add its own variables. Avoid current package-size or environment-count claims from an older snapshot.

slides.title: Four roles. Two families.
slides.notes: Now the audience has seen the features: name the plugin contracts just before the authoring example. At most one plugin fills each role: type_ops, func_entry, ast_preprocessor and compiler. decorators and adapters are families containing any number of plugins. Eight shipped plugins: TypeOps, func.Entry, scf.ASTPreprocessor, execution_engine.Compiler, gpu.Kernels, PyTorchPlugin, DlpackPlugin, TvmFfiPlugin. arith, vector and llvm are operation modules composed by TypeOps, not three more plugins. Plugin itself only supplies available/install/shared_libs/register_dialects lifecycle. The sub-DSL owns pipeline(); plugins do not contribute pass lists.
slides.caption: Eight shipped plugins. Op modules are not plugins.

slides.title: 15 · One subclass. One Plugins record.
slides.notes: This is the current assembly shape, not the obsolete list-valued plugins API. Import BaseDSL and Plugins from mlir.dsl; plugins from their role/family packages. Modules arith/vector/llvm are arguments to TypeOps, not independent plugins. Constructor, namespace exports and pipeline are shown/discussed next. A custom DSL should depend on the core and selected plugins rather than importing the reference language.

left.label: Downstream DSL · implementation excerpt
left.code:
class MyDSL(BaseDSL):
    plugins = Plugins(
        type_ops=TypeOps(
            scalars=arith, vectors=vector, memory=llvm),
        func_entry=func.Entry(),
        ast_preprocessor=scf.ASTPreprocessor(),
        compiler=execution_engine.Compiler(),
        decorators=[gpu.Kernels()],
        adapters=[pytorch.PyTorchPlugin()],
    )

slides.title: Own the namespace and lowering
slides.notes: These are methods on MyDSL from the previous slide. mydsl exports the chosen user types, jit/kernel/compile names and syntax helpers its preprocessor imports. name selects MY_DSL_* configuration. The example pass list is schematic: mydialect and its lowering are downstream definitions, not shipped names; include vector/math/GPU passes if those operations are emitted. The concrete reference pass list is in mlir_dsl.py. No plugin publishes passes.

left.label: Downstream DSL · methods
left.code:
def __init__(self):
    super().__init__(
        name="MY_DSL",
        dsl_package_name=["mydsl"],
        preprocess=True)

def register_dialects(self, ctx):
    mydialect.register_dialect(ctx)

slides.title: Reuse a composition; change one field
slides.notes: This exact variant pattern is in example11. replace creates a new frozen Plugins record; role implementations are retained while decorators and adapters are dropped. Each DSL instance shallow-copies and installs its available plugins. Inheriting a decorator attribute from a base class does not make its missing plugin available; invoking it reports CALL_PLUGIN_REQUIRED. A separately authored language can instead construct BaseDSL and its record from scratch.

left.label: Python · implementation excerpt
left.code:
from dataclasses import replace

class CpuOnly(m.MlirTestDSL):
    plugins = replace(
        m.MlirTestDSL.plugins,
        decorators=(),
        adapters=(),
    )

slides.title: Every plugin has a small shared lifecycle
slides.notes: Only these hooks are on bare Plugin. A role or family adds its own contract. Unavailable plugins are dropped and listed in unavailable_plugins; available ones are copied/installed in record order: roles, decorators, adapters. Each dispatch loop calls its own role/family. Compiler, decorator and adapter hooks must not be described as a single universal plugin interface.

slides.title: One program: Python recipe + staged loop
slides.notes: The array loop is staged and the ordinary recipe dictionary dispatches at trace time. Pointer load/store operations use the selected type_ops memory module; arithmetic uses its scalar module. The current v14 metaprogram check produced [6,9,12,15] for [0,1,2,3] with AddN(2), MulN(3). The displayed IR is a loop-body excerpt. This ties together values, metaprogramming, memory, control flow and execution.

left.label: Python · executed

right.label: MLIR · loop body
right.code:
%p = llvm.getelementptr %arr[%i]
    : (!llvm.ptr, i32) -> !llvm.ptr, f32
%x = llvm.load %p : !llvm.ptr -> f32
%a = arith.addf %x, %two : f32
%r = arith.mulf %a, %three : f32
llvm.store %r, %p : f32, !llvm.ptr
scf.yield

slides.takeaway: Staged array loop · Meta recipe loop

slides.title: Tile IR: choose target implementations
slides.notes: Proposed mapping of a downstream Tile backend to the current role/family architecture. The tile.* classes are illustrative interfaces, not shipped or executed implementations. The existing DkgDSL backend motivates the mapping but has not been ported here. Reuse the core and compatible existing adapters; replace the target-specific roles and decorator plugin. All five closing slides are a five-minute design sketch.

left.label: Downstream port sketch · proposed API
left.code:
class TileDSL(BaseDSL):
    plugins = Plugins(
        type_ops=tile.TypeOps(),
        func_entry=tile.Entry(),
        ast_preprocessor=tile.ASTPreprocessor(),
        compiler=tile.Compiler(),
        decorators=[tile.Kernels()],
        adapters=[dlpack.DlpackPlugin()],
    )

slides.title: Tile IR: one type-ops role
slides.notes: The type_ops contract covers scalar, vector and pointer types/operations. A real Tile implementation must provide the relevant hooks and preserve dtype policy. The checked rank-zero tensor example demonstrates replacement of physical representation but is not CUDA Tile IR and has no real Tile lowering. This slide is a proposed downstream mapping, not an executed port.

slides.title: Tile IR: choose its control-flow model
slides.notes: The Tile preprocessor and region callbacks are proposed downstream definitions. CUDA Tile loop can use its own early-exit constructs; the current shipped SCF preprocessor rejects data-dependent early exits, and simply swapping one callback is not a promise of complete support. Different target semantics may need a different rewrite. No legacy annotation wrappers are used.

left.label: Downstream port sketch · proposed API

slides.title: Tile IR: keep a small user surface
slides.notes: Illustrative target namespace and directly typed Tensor annotations, not a current executable tile API. A downstream module emits the target operations, the type-ops role routes operators, and the decorator plugin/launcher supplies the target entry and launch model. Direct typed annotations are used. The kernel body is an API sketch; real indices, shapes and memory operations are target-defined.

left.label: Downstream port sketch · user API
left.code:
@tile.kernel
def add(a: tile.Tensor,
        b: tile.Tensor,
        out: tile.Tensor):
    x = tile.load(a)
    y = tile.load(b)
    tile.store(out, x + y)

right.label: Proposed plugin ownership
right.code:
tile.TypeOps
  types + operations

tile.Kernels
  entry + launch

tile.Compiler

slides.title: Tile IR: the target owns launch
slides.notes: The desired downstream path can launch a decorated kernel directly from Python using a target launcher. The kernel decorator plugin owns that behavior; the compiler role can return a target artifact rather than ExecutionEngine. CUDA Python is a proposed launch mechanism, not implemented or GPU-tested by this deck. This differs from the shipped GPU plugin whose kernel calls are launched from @jit through gpu.launch_func. Close by returning to the four use cases: same core, selected roles, own pipeline.
